title: The Valuation Habit Most Owners Skip Until They're Already Trying to Sell
linkedin:
Most business owners find out what their business is worth exactly once, the week they decide to sell it.

By then the number is just information. There's no runway left to act on anything it reveals.

Here's the pattern we see across owner-led businesses: most owners arrive at that first valuation with a number already fixed in their head, usually a multiple of revenue overheard at an industry event or picked up from a competitor's rumoured sale price.

That guess is almost never close. A revenue multiple ignores the one variable that actually decides price, which is how much of that revenue converts into earnings a new owner could rely on without the founder in the room.

The businesses that handle this well treat the valuation differently. They get the number on an ordinary Tuesday, with no sale anywhere in sight, and use it as a diagnostic rather than a verdict.

Customer concentration takes the better part of a year to fix properly. Reducing owner dependence takes longer again. None of that work can start the week a sale process does, because by then the business is being presented, not rebuilt.

Get the same number eighteen months earlier and it stops being a post-mortem. It becomes a ranked list of exactly what to fix first, while there's still time to fix it.

October is a sensible moment for that check. EOFY figures have settled, the numbers are clean, and Christmas trading pressure is still a few months off.

Honest question for business owners: do you actually know what your business is worth right now, today, with no sale in the works?

Most owners don't. The first time anyone puts a real number on the business is usually the week they decide to sell, which means there's no time left to do anything useful with what it shows.

The owners who handle this best check the number well before they need it, while there's still time to fix whatever it turns up. Worth doing before you're under pressure to, not after.

A note for business owners across Brisbane, Queensland and the wider East Coast as Australian Small Business Month winds down for another year.

Most owners only ever find out what their business is worth once, and it's usually the week they've already decided to sell. By then, the number is just information. There's no time left to act on anything it reveals about the business.

A valuation taken well before any sale is on the table works differently. It shows plainly which parts of the business carry real value and which parts only look like they do day to day, things like how concentrated the revenue is across customers, or how much of the earnings would hold up if the owner stepped back for a few months.

Those issues typically take twelve to eighteen months of steady work to fix properly, which is exactly why knowing the number early matters. Late October sits in a useful spot on the calendar for this, with EOFY figures settled and clean, and Christmas trading still a little way off.

None of this requires any decision to sell. It just requires a willingness to find out the real figure rather than the one you're assuming.

Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog for a closer look at what a valuation reveals and when to get one done.
